# Q10: What Are Bridge Methods?

[Home](../../README.md) > [Generics & Type System](./README.md) > Bridge Methods

---

## 🟠 Difficulty: Advanced

## Question
> What are bridge methods in Java? Why does the compiler generate them?

---

## Quick Answer
**Bridge methods** are synthetic methods generated by the Java compiler to preserve **polymorphism** after type erasure. When a generic class is extended and a method is overridden with a more specific type, erasure changes the method signature — the overriding method no longer matches the erased parent method. The compiler inserts a bridge method with the erased signature that delegates to the actual overriding method, maintaining correct virtual dispatch.

---

## Detailed Explanation

### The Problem: Erasure Breaks Overriding

```java
// Generic parent class
public class Box<T> {
    private T value;

    public T getValue() { return value; }

    public void setValue(T value) { this.value = value; }
}

// Concrete subclass with specific type
public class StringBox extends Box<String> {

    @Override
    public String getValue() {     // Returns String, not Object
        return super.getValue();
    }

    @Override
    public void setValue(String value) {  // Accepts String, not Object
        super.setValue(value);
    }
}
```

### After Type Erasure

```java
// Box<T> erases to:
public class Box {
    private Object value;
    public Object getValue() { return value; }       // erased: Object
    public void setValue(Object value) { this.value = value; } // erased: Object
}

// StringBox erases to:
public class StringBox extends Box {
    public String getValue() { return (String) super.getValue(); }
    // ⚠️ This is getValue() → String, NOT getValue() → Object
    // It no longer overrides Box.getValue() → Object!

    public void setValue(String value) { super.setValue(value); }
    // ⚠️ This is setValue(String), NOT setValue(Object)
    // It no longer overrides Box.setValue(Object)!
}
```

### The Solution: Bridge Methods

```java
// The compiler generates bridge methods in StringBox:
public class StringBox extends Box {

    // YOUR method (actual implementation)
    public String getValue() {
        return (String) super.getValue();
    }

    // BRIDGE method (compiler-generated)
    // Overrides Box.getValue() → Object
    public Object getValue() {        // ← Bridge: matches erased parent
        return this.getValue();        // ← Delegates to your String version
    }

    // YOUR method
    public void setValue(String value) {
        super.setValue(value);
    }

    // BRIDGE method (compiler-generated)
    // Overrides Box.setValue(Object)
    public void setValue(Object value) {  // ← Bridge: matches erased parent
        this.setValue((String) value);    // ← Delegates with cast
    }
}
```

### Visualizing Bridge Method Delegation

```
Polymorphic call: box.setValue("hello")
  │
  ├── At compile time: calls setValue(Object)  [erased signature]
  │
  └── At runtime (StringBox instance):
        │
        ├── Bridge method: setValue(Object value)
        │     └── delegates to → setValue((String) value)
        │
        └── Your method: setValue(String value)
              └── executes your code
```

### Viewing Bridge Methods with javap

```bash
# Compile the classes
javac Box.java StringBox.java

# Disassemble StringBox to see bridge methods
javap -c -p StringBox.class
```

**Output shows:**

```
public class StringBox extends Box {
  // Your method
  public java.lang.String getValue();
    Code: ...

  // Bridge method — ACC_BRIDGE flag set
  public java.lang.Object getValue();
    Code:
       0: aload_0
       1: invokevirtual #2  // calls StringBox.getValue():String
       4: areturn

  // Your method
  public void setValue(java.lang.String);
    Code: ...

  // Bridge method — ACC_BRIDGE flag set
  public void setValue(java.lang.Object);
    Code:
       0: aload_0
       1: aload_1
       2: checkcast     #3  // cast to String
       5: invokevirtual #4  // calls StringBox.setValue(String)
       8: return
}
```

### Detecting Bridge Methods via Reflection

```java
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.lang.reflect.Modifier;

public class BridgeInspector {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Method method : StringBox.class.getDeclaredMethods()) {
            System.out.printf("%-30s bridge=%s  synthetic=%s%n",
                method.toGenericString(),
                method.isBridge(),      // true for bridge methods
                method.isSynthetic()    // bridge methods are also synthetic
            );
        }
    }
}

// Output:
// public String StringBox.getValue()        bridge=false  synthetic=false
// public Object StringBox.getValue()        bridge=true   synthetic=true
// public void StringBox.setValue(String)     bridge=false  synthetic=false
// public void StringBox.setValue(Object)     bridge=true   synthetic=true
```

### Bridge Methods with Comparable

```java
public class SortableItem implements Comparable<SortableItem> {
    private int value;

    public SortableItem(int value) { this.value = value; }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(SortableItem other) {  // Your method
        return Integer.compare(this.value, other.value);
    }

    // Compiler generates bridge method:
    // public int compareTo(Object other) {       // Bridge
    //     return compareTo((SortableItem) other); // Delegates with cast
    // }
}

// Why needed? Comparable<T> erases to Comparable (raw):
// interface Comparable {
//     int compareTo(Object o);  // Erased signature
// }
// Your compareTo(SortableItem) doesn't match compareTo(Object)
// Bridge method fills the gap
```

### Bridge Methods with Covariant Return Types

```java
public class Animal {
    public Animal create() {
        return new Animal();
    }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public Dog create() {       // Covariant return (Dog, not Animal)
        return new Dog();
    }

    // Bridge method generated:
    // public Animal create() {   // Matches parent's return type
    //     return this.create();  // Delegates to Dog create()
    // }
}

// This is actually how covariant returns work in the JVM:
// The JVM doesn't support covariant returns natively
// Bridge methods make it work!
```

### Bridge Methods and ClassCastException

```java
// Bridge methods can cause unexpected ClassCastException

Box<String> stringBox = new StringBox();
Box rawBox = stringBox;  // Raw type — loses type safety

// The bridge method in StringBox.setValue(Object) casts to String:
rawBox.setValue(42);  // 💥 ClassCastException at bridge method's cast!

// The bridge method does: setValue((String) 42) → ClassCastException
// This is actually GOOD — it catches the type violation at the point of entry
```

### ACC_BRIDGE and ACC_SYNTHETIC Flags

```java
// Bridge methods have two JVM flags:
// ACC_BRIDGE    (0x0040) — marks it as a bridge method
// ACC_SYNTHETIC (0x1000) — marks it as compiler-generated

// These flags are used by:
// - Method.isBridge()    → checks ACC_BRIDGE
// - Method.isSynthetic() → checks ACC_SYNTHETIC
// - Frameworks (Spring, Hibernate) to skip bridge methods
// - javadoc to hide bridge methods from documentation

// Spring Framework uses BridgeMethodResolver:
import org.springframework.core.BridgeMethodResolver;

Method bridgeMethod = /* ... */;
Method actualMethod = BridgeMethodResolver.findBridgedMethod(bridgeMethod);
// Returns the non-bridge method that the bridge delegates to
```

### Multiple Bridge Methods

```java
public interface Transformer<I, O> {
    O transform(I input);
}

public class StringToInt implements Transformer<String, Integer> {
    @Override
    public Integer transform(String input) {
        return Integer.parseInt(input);
    }

    // TWO bridge methods generated:
    // 1. Bridge for return type:
    //    public Object transform(String input) {
    //        return this.transform(input);  // boxes Integer to Object
    //    }
    //
    // 2. Bridge for parameter AND return type:
    //    public Object transform(Object input) {
    //        return this.transform((String) input);
    //    }
}
```

---

## Anti-Patterns

```java
// ❌ Filtering methods without considering bridges
for (Method m : clazz.getDeclaredMethods()) {
    process(m);  // Will process bridge methods too!
}

// ❌ Assuming only one version of an overridden method exists
Method[] methods = StringBox.class.getDeclaredMethods();
// Contains BOTH getValue():String AND getValue():Object

// ❌ Using raw types causes bridge method ClassCastException
Box rawBox = new StringBox();
rawBox.setValue(42);  // 💥 Bridge method casts to String
```

## Best Practices

```java
// ✅ Filter out bridge methods in reflection code
for (Method method : clazz.getDeclaredMethods()) {
    if (!method.isBridge()) {
        process(method);  // Only process real methods
    }
}

// ✅ Use Spring's BridgeMethodResolver in framework code
Method resolved = BridgeMethodResolver.findBridgedMethod(method);

// ✅ Understand that bridge methods maintain the type safety contract
// They insert casts that catch type violations early

// ✅ Know that bridge methods are an implementation detail
// You never write them — the compiler generates them automatically
// Your code should work correctly without thinking about them

// ✅ Use @Override to ensure your method truly overrides
@Override
public String getValue() {  // Compiler verifies this overrides Box.getValue()
    return super.getValue();
}
```

---

## Interview Tips
- Bridge methods are **compiler-generated synthetic** methods
- They exist to maintain **polymorphism** after type erasure
- You can detect them via `Method.isBridge()` and `Method.isSynthetic()`
- Covariant return types also rely on bridge methods (JVM doesn't support them natively)
- `javap -c -p` reveals bridge methods in bytecode
- Spring's `BridgeMethodResolver` resolves bridge → actual method mapping
- Bridge methods insert **casts** that can throw `ClassCastException` when raw types are misused
